rw: Gross pay is hourly rate times hours worked: $15 x 20 = $300. Gross pay is the total earned before taxes and other deductions are taken out.

ww.$35: $35 comes from adding the hours and the rate (15 + 20) instead of multiplying them, so it ignores that pay grows with every hour worked.
ww.$3,000: $3,000 is far too high; it looks like 15 x 200 or an extra zero added, but 20 hours at $15 cannot produce that much weekly pay.
ww.$150: $150 is only half the correct amount; it would be 10 hours at $15. Jordan worked 20 hours, so the pay is 15 x 20 = $300.

rw: The W-4 lets a new employee state filing status and allowances or adjustments so the employer withholds the right federal income tax from each paycheck.

ww.1099: A 1099 reports income paid to independent contractors, not employees, and it is not used to set income tax withholding for a new hire.
ww.W-2: The W-2 is issued by the employer after the year ends to report wages and taxes withheld, so it does not set withholding for a new hire.
ww.I-9: The I-9 verifies identity and legal authorization to work in the United States. It has nothing to do with how much income tax is withheld.

rw: Social Security tax is part of FICA, which federal law requires employers to withhold from nearly every paycheck, with the employer paying a matching share.

ww.A charity donation: A charity donation through payroll is voluntary; the employee chooses to give, so it is not a deduction the law requires.
ww.Union dues paid out: Union dues are set by a union agreement and paid by members, not required by law for every worker, so this is not a legal deduction.
ww.A voluntary pension: A voluntary pension or retirement contribution is the employee's choice by definition, so it is not a deduction the law forces on every worker.

rw: Gross pay per paycheck is annual salary divided by pay periods: $36,000 / 26 is about $1,385, before taxes and other deductions are subtracted.

ww.$3,000: $3,000 is the 12 month figure ($36,000 / 12 = $3,000), but Marcus is paid 26 times a year, so each paycheck is much smaller.
ww.$692: $692 is about half of the right amount; it comes from dividing by 52 weekly periods. The question says 26 biweekly paychecks, so use 26.
ww.$1,500: $1,500 comes from dividing by 24 pay periods, as for a twice monthly schedule. Marcus is paid every two weeks, which is 26 periods, so the result is $1,385.

rw: Stronger job skills make workers more valuable to employers, which usually leads to better pay, promotions and more job options over a career.

ww.Automatic loan approval: Skills do not trigger automatic loan approval; lenders look at credit history, income and debts, not whether a person learned new skills.
ww.Lower job opportunities: More skills tend to widen the set of jobs a person qualifies for, so job opportunities rise rather than fall.
ww.Fewer chances to be promoted: Skills usually make promotion more likely, since employers advance workers who can handle bigger responsibilities. Fewer chances would be the opposite of the real effect.

rw: Passive income comes from assets such as interest, dividends or rental property with little ongoing work, which is why it matches the description in the question.

ww.Tip earnings: Tips are earned by serving customers, so they are active income tied to work performed, not money produced by an asset.
ww.Sales commissions: Sales commissions are a percentage of sales a worker makes, so they depend on regular selling work and are active earned income.
ww.Hourly wages: Hourly wages are paid for time worked on the job, which makes them active income rather than money earned from an asset.

rw: A share of stock is a unit of ownership, so shareholders own part of the company and may earn dividends or gains if its value rises.

ww.An insurance policy for losses: An insurance policy transfers risk of loss to an insurer in exchange for premiums. A share of stock is not a policy and does not cover losses.
ww.A loan from an investor to a firm: A loan from an investor to a firm describes a bond, where the investor is a lender. A stock holder is an owner, not a lender.
ww.A savings account at a local bank: A savings account at a bank holds deposits and pays interest, usually insured. Stock is ownership in a company with no guaranteed value.

rw: A bond is a loan from an investor to a company or government, which repays the principal on a set date and pays interest along the way.

ww.A share of ownership in a company that i: Ownership of a company is a share of stock, not a bond. Bondholders are lenders and do not own part of the issuer.
ww.A fee a bank charges on an account below: A fee for falling below a minimum balance is a bank account charge, not an investment. A bond is a loan that pays the holder interest.
ww.A type of tax paid on investment income: Taxes on investment income are paid to the government and are not an investment product. A bond is a debt security that earns interest for the lender.

rw: By owning many different investments, a loss in any single one has a smaller effect on the total. This reduces firm specific risk, though not market risk.

ww.Inflation completely for every investor: Diversification cannot remove inflation, which affects the buying power of all money and every investor; it only spreads out the risk among holdings.
ww.Every kind of risk that investors face: Diversifying cannot eliminate every risk, such as market wide downturns that hit most investments at once. It mainly reduces the risk tied to any one holding.
ww.All taxes owed on investment income: Diversification does not change taxes owed; investment income is taxed according to tax law no matter how many different holdings an investor has.

rw: Simple interest equals principal x rate x time: $1,000 x 0.05 x 3 = $150, the same $50 added each year with no compounding.

ww.$1,150: $1,150 would add the principal to $150, or use compound growth with extra years. The question asks only for the interest earned, not the final balance.
ww.$50: $50 is one year of interest (5 percent of $1,000). The investment runs 3 years, so the interest must be multiplied by 3.
ww.$157.63: $157.63 is the compound interest result (1,000 x 1.05 cubed minus 1,000). The question states simple interest, which does not earn interest on interest.

rw: U.S. Treasury bonds are backed by the full faith and credit of the federal government, so default risk is very low, making them among the safest investments.

ww.Start-up company shares: Start up shares are highly risky because many new companies fail, so investors can lose their entire investment. They are not a low risk choice.
ww.Speculative tokens: Speculative tokens are volatile digital assets whose prices swing widely with little underlying value, so they sit among the highest risk choices.
ww.Penny stock shares: Penny stocks are low priced shares of small companies that trade thinly and swing sharply, so they carry far more risk than government bonds.

rw: A mutual fund pools money from many investors and a manager buys a mix of stocks, bonds or other securities, giving small investors built in diversification.

ww.One company's share held by one investor: A single company's share held by one investor is direct stock ownership. A mutual fund instead pools money from many investors into one portfolio.
ww.A bank loan used to buy a house or a new: A bank loan used to buy a house or car is a mortgage or auto loan, which is borrowing, not an investment fund that holds securities.
ww.A government grant given to small busine: A government grant is money given to small businesses for a purpose and is not repaid. A mutual fund is an investment pooled from investors.

rw: Returns earn further returns, so more years allow the growth to build on itself. This is compounding, which makes early investing so powerful.

ww.Investments never lose any value: Investments can and do lose value, especially in the short run, so claiming they never lose any value is false, and early investing does not change that.
ww.No taxes are owed on early gains: Gains are generally taxable whenever they are realized, or as dividends and interest are earned, so starting early does not erase taxes owed.
ww.Fees are always zero at the start: Funds, brokers and accounts can charge fees from the very start, so starting early does not make fees zero. Compounding is the real advantage.

rw: A credit score summarizes credit history, such as paying on time, how much is owed and credit age, to show how reliably a person repays debts.

ww.A person's yearly income from work: Income is not part of the score calculation; lenders may check income separately. Scores reflect how debts were handled, not how much a person earns.
ww.The interest rate on all of their loans: The interest rate on loans is set by lenders, partly based on the score, but the score does not simply report the rate on all of someone's loans.
ww.The balance in a savings account at a ba: Savings account balances are not reported to credit bureaus, so they do not appear in a score. The score reflects borrowing and repayment behavior.

rw: Payment history is the largest factor in a credit score, so paying every bill on time builds a record of reliability that lenders value.

ww.Using the full limit on every card: Using the full limit on every card gives a high utilization ratio, which hurts the score. Experts suggest staying well below about 30 percent of limits.
ww.Missing a payment now and then: Missed payments are reported to credit bureaus and lower the score, since payment history is the biggest part of credit scoring.
ww.Applying for many new cards at once: Many new applications create hard inquiries and lower the average age of accounts, which can lower the score. Credit should be added gradually.

rw: APR, or annual percentage rate, shows the yearly cost of borrowing as a percentage, including interest and some fees. At 24 percent, $100 owed costs about $24 a year.

ww.The card's credit limit set by the bank: The credit limit is the maximum balance the issuer allows, which is a separate term from APR, which only measures the cost of borrowing.
ww.The yearly fee for owning the card with: An annual fee is a separate charge, while APR measures the cost of borrowing as a yearly percentage. A card can have a high APR and no annual fee.
ww.The minimum monthly payment you must mak: The minimum payment is the smallest amount due each month, set by the issuer, and is separate from APR, which is the yearly borrowing cost.

rw: Monthly interest is balance times monthly rate: $500 x 0.02 = $10. With no payment made, that interest is added to the balance owed.

ww.$100: $100 would be 20 percent of $500, ten times the real rate. At 2 percent monthly the charge is much smaller, since 0.02 x 500 is $10.
ww.$1: $1 is only 0.2 percent of $500, so it is a tenth of the correct amount. At 2 percent, 500 x 0.02 equals $10.
ww.$50: $50 would be a 10 percent monthly rate, five times the stated 2 percent. The correct figure is 500 x 0.02 = $10.

rw: Paying the full statement balance by the due date usually keeps the grace period, so purchases are never charged interest on the card.

ww.Paying only the minimum amount due each: Paying only the minimum leaves most of the balance, so interest keeps accumulating on it. This is the slowest and most expensive way to repay.
ww.Skipping a payment every now and then to: Skipping payments brings late fees, penalty rates and credit score damage, and interest keeps accruing, so it never saves money.
ww.Taking cash advances to cover other bill: Cash advances usually start charging interest right away with no grace period and carry extra fees, so they add interest instead of avoiding it.

rw: Payday lenders make short term, small loans with fees that equal annual rates of 300 percent or more, among the costliest forms of credit.

ww.A credit union: Credit unions are member owned nonprofits that typically offer lower interest rates than most other lenders, so they are not the costliest option.
ww.Student loan agency: Student loans from agencies often have capped or federally set rates, which are usually lower than short term consumer loans like payday loans.
ww.A mortgage bank: A mortgage is secured by the home and usually has a lower rate than unsecured loans, so mortgage banks are not the highest priced lenders.

rw: A secured loan is backed by collateral, such as a car or house, that the lender can take (repossess) if the borrower defaults, lowering the lender's risk.

ww.A loan guaranteed only by the borrower's: A loan backed only by a verbal promise has no collateral and is unsecured by nature. A secured loan requires pledging an asset.
ww.A loan with no interest that must be rep: A one day loan with no interest is not a standard loan product, and a secured loan is defined by collateral, not by interest or repayment time.
ww.A loan that charges no interest and requ: A loan with no interest and no repayment promise would effectively be a gift. A secured loan is a real debt with collateral behind it.

rw: Insurance transfers the chance of a large loss to an insurer, which pools many customers' premiums and pays covered claims, such as accidents or medical bills.

ww.A savings plan that guarantees a return: Insurance does not guarantee a return on savings; it pays out only when a covered loss happens. A savings plan is a different financial product.
ww.A type of loan that must be repaid with: A loan gives money now to be repaid with interest. Insurance instead pays claims for covered losses and is paid for with premiums.
ww.A tax refund paid by the government each: A tax refund is money the government returns after a tax filing and not every taxpayer gets one. It has no link to insurance coverage.

rw: A deductible is the amount the policyholder pays out of pocket on a covered claim before the insurer starts paying its share of costs.

ww.The maximum amount the insurer will ever: The maximum an insurer will pay is the policy limit, a different term. A deductible is what you pay first, not the cap on payout.
ww.A refund of premiums for coverage that w: Premiums are not refunded just because a policy went unused, and a deductible is an out of pocket cost on a claim, not a refund.
ww.The monthly payment that is made to the: The monthly payment to the insurer is the premium. The deductible is paid only when a claim is made, before coverage begins.

rw: Health insurance pays all or part of medical costs such as doctor visits, hospital stays and prescriptions, in exchange for premiums plus deductibles and copays.

ww.Auto insurance: Auto insurance covers vehicle damage and liability from car accidents. It may include limited medical payments but is not meant for general medical expenses.
ww.Life insurance: Life insurance pays a death benefit to beneficiaries when the insured person dies. It does not cover the insured person's medical bills.
ww.Renter's insurance: Renter's insurance covers a tenant's belongings and liability for the rented home, not medical expenses for illness or injury.

rw: With a higher deductible Casey pays more on a claim but the insurer's risk drops, so the premium is lower. It suits people with savings to cover the gap.

ww.A higher premium and a lower cost in a c: A higher deductible usually lowers the premium, since the insured takes on more risk. A higher premium paired with lower claim costs describes a low deductible instead.
ww.Coverage for all damage with no limits o: A deductible does not extend coverage to everything; policies still have limits and exclusions, and a higher deductible only shifts more cost to the driver.
ww.No change in the premium or the cost of: Changing the deductible changes both sides: the premium goes down and the cost paid on a claim goes up. They do not stay the same.

rw: Strong, unique passwords make accounts hard to guess or crack, and one breach will not expose other accounts. This lowers the risk of identity theft.

ww.Reusing one password everywhere: Reusing one password lets a thief who gets it from one breach log in to every other account, which raises the risk of identity theft.
ww.Posting your birth date publicly: A public birth date gives thieves a key detail to answer security questions or open accounts in your name, increasing identity theft risk.
ww.Sharing your PIN with friends: A PIN should be kept private; sharing it lets others access accounts and cards, which makes fraud and identity theft more likely.

rw: Renter's insurance covers the tenant's personal property from losses like theft or fire and gives liability coverage if someone is hurt in the unit.

ww.The tenant's credit score history: Credit history is tracked by credit bureaus, and renter's insurance does not protect or change a tenant's score. It covers physical belongings and liability.
ww.The building's structure and walls: The building structure is the landlord's responsibility and is covered by the landlord's own property policy, not by a tenant's renter's insurance.
ww.The landlord's income from rent: Renter's insurance does not replace rent income for a landlord. A landlord would need a separate landlord policy to cover lost rental income.

rw: An emergency fund covers surprises like car repairs or job loss, so you avoid borrowing on credit cards or loans and paying interest.

ww.To invest in risky stocks for higher ret: Risky stocks can lose value quickly, so they are a poor place for money needed in an emergency. An emergency fund should be safe and available.
ww.To pay for vacations that have been plan: Vacations are planned wants, not unexpected expenses. Planned spending should come from a separate savings goal, not the emergency fund.
ww.To avoid ever needing to buy any insuran: An emergency fund does not replace insurance; many large losses, such as a major accident or illness, can exceed any savings, so coverage is still needed.

rw: A savings account keeps money safe, usually insured, and pays interest, so the balance grows while staying accessible for future needs.

ww.To buy stocks and bonds each week: Buying stocks and bonds is investing, which is done through brokerage accounts. A savings account is mainly for safe storage, not weekly trading.
ww.To borrow money from a bank at once: Borrowing from a bank is a loan, which creates debt. A savings account holds your own money and pays you interest.
ww.To pay bills automatically each month: Automatic bill payments are typically handled from a checking account. The main purpose of savings is to store money and earn interest.

rw: Compound interest is calculated on the deposit plus the interest already earned, so the balance grows faster the longer it stays in the account.

ww.Interest earned only on the original dep: Interest only on the original deposit is simple interest. Compound interest also earns interest on interest already added, so it grows faster.
ww.A fee for opening an account at a local: An account opening fee is a bank charge, not a type of interest. Compound interest is earnings that are added to the balance.
ww.Interest charged only once at the start: Interest charged once at the start is not compounding. Compounding repeats on a schedule, with each period's interest earning more interest.

rw: Simple interest equals principal x rate x time: $200 x 0.03 x 1 = $6. After one year the total would be $206.

ww.$206: $206 is the final balance (200 + 6), not the interest. The question asks only how much interest is earned, which is $6.
ww.$60: $60 is ten times too large; it comes from misplacing a decimal. Three percent of $200 is 200 x 0.03 = $6.
ww.$0.60: $0.60 is ten times too small. Converting 3 percent to 0.03 and multiplying by $200 gives $6, not 60 cents.

rw: Setting a target and automating a fixed transfer each payday builds the fund steadily and removes the temptation to skip. It is a proven way to start saving.

ww.Wait until money is left at month end be: Waiting for leftover money usually means nothing is saved, since spending expands to fill income. Saving should come first, not last.
ww.Put all of your savings money into one s: Putting all savings in one risky stock could wipe out the fund. An emergency fund needs safety and easy access, not risk.
ww.Spend first and then save whatever is le: Spending first and saving what is left is the opposite of paying yourself first. There often is little left, so the fund never grows.

rw: FDIC insurance protects deposits such as savings and checking accounts at insured banks, up to $250,000 per depositor, per bank, per ownership category.

ww.A cryptocurrency wallet on a phone: A crypto wallet is not a bank deposit, so FDIC insurance does not cover it. Crypto prices swing widely and losses are not insured.
ww.A personal loan made to a friend: A personal loan to a friend is an informal debt with no insurance. If the friend does not repay, no agency covers the loss.
ww.Shares held in a stock brokerage account: Brokerage accounts may have SIPC protection against broker failure, but not FDIC insurance, and it does not cover investment losses from market declines.

rw: Dividing 72 by the annual interest rate estimates the years needed to double money. At 6 percent, money doubles in about 12 years.

ww.How much income tax a person owes in a s: Income tax owed depends on tax brackets, deductions and credits, not on the Rule of 72, which only estimates how fast money doubles.
ww.The best age at which a person should re: The Rule of 72 has no connection to retirement age. It is a quick math shortcut for growth of money at a given interest rate.
ww.The monthly payment that is due on a loa: Loan payments come from payment formulas involving the amount, rate and term. The Rule of 72 estimates doubling time, not a monthly payment.

rw: Saving $600 in six months by setting aside $100 a month has an amount, a deadline and a plan ($100 x 6 = $600), so it is specific and measurable.

ww.Save more money at some point in the fut: Saving more at some point in the future is vague, with no amount or date, so progress cannot be measured. A good goal needs both.
ww.Spend a lot less on the things that you: Spending a lot less is not measurable because it gives no number or timeframe to check, so a person cannot tell whether the goal was met.
ww.Become wealthy by the time that you are: Becoming wealthy later has no amount, no deadline and no plan, which makes it a wish rather than a specific, measurable goal.

rw: A budget is a plan for how to use income by assigning money to expenses, savings and goals, so spending can be tracked against the plan.

ww.A bank account for savings: A savings account is a place to hold money at a bank. A budget is a plan for spending and saving, not an account.
ww.A type of tax on your income: Income tax is a government charge on earnings. A budget is a personal plan and is not a tax at all.
ww.A list of past debts only: Looking only at past debts would ignore income and future spending. A budget is a forward looking plan covering income, expenses and savings.

rw: Monthly rent is the same amount each month under a lease, which makes it a fixed expense that is predictable when budgeting.

ww.Movie tickets: Movie tickets are a discretionary, variable expense that changes depending on how often you go, so they are not a fixed expense.
ww.Gift money: Gift money varies by occasion and is optional, so it changes from month to month and is not a fixed expense.
ww.Restaurant meals: Restaurant meals change with how often you eat out and what you order, which makes them a variable, discretionary expense.

rw: The 50/30/20 rule sets 50 percent of income for needs: $2,000 x 0.50 = $1,000. The rest is 30 percent for wants and 20 percent for savings.

ww.$600: $600 is 30 percent of $2,000, the share the 50/30/20 rule gives to wants, not to needs.
ww.$400: $400 is 20 percent of $2,000, the savings and debt portion of the rule. Needs get the larger 50 percent share, or $1,000.
ww.$1,400: $1,400 is 70 percent, which would combine needs and wants. The rule gives needs only 50 percent, so $2,000 x 0.50 = $1,000.

rw: Unit price per ounce puts different sized boxes on equal footing, so you can see which gives more cereal for the money.

ww.Choose the one with a popular mascot: A popular mascot is marketing, not value. It tells you nothing about the cost per ounce and can push buyers toward worse deals.
ww.Compare the sizes of the boxes: A bigger box is not always cheaper per ounce, so comparing sizes alone does not show which one gives the better value.
ww.Compare the brand names only: Brand names alone do not show cost. Two brands can differ widely in price per ounce, so name comparison ignores the real price.

rw: Comparison shopping means checking prices, features and quality across several sellers so you can pick the best value for your money.

ww.Buying the first item that you happen to: Buying the first item you see skips any comparison, so you may overpay or miss better options. That is the opposite of comparison shopping.
ww.Buying an item on impulse with no planni: Impulse buying means purchasing without a plan, which is the opposite of comparing options to find the best price or quality.
ww.Paying only in cash instead of using a c: How you pay, cash or card, is a payment method and has nothing to do with comparing sellers on price and features.

rw: A 24 hour wait gives time for the urge to fade and lets you decide whether the item is really needed, which cuts down impulse purchases.

ww.Using store credit freely whenever you a: Store credit encourages spur of the moment purchases without paying right away, so it increases impulse buying rather than controlling it.
ww.Browsing online sale sites every single: Browsing sale sites daily exposes you to constant temptation and promotions, which increases impulse buying instead of controlling it.
ww.Shopping for non-essentials while you ar: Shopping while hungry or emotional weakens self control, and studies show people buy more. It encourages impulse buying, not limits it.

rw: Needs come before wants in a budget. Lunch is a need, so Leo covers it first and spends only what is left on the headphones.

ww.Buy the headphones first and worry about: Buying wants first while skipping needs puts a basic need at risk. A want should never come before food.
ww.Split the money evenly between lunch and: Splitting evenly treats a need and a want as equal, but needs have priority, and half of $50 on headphones may leave lunch underfunded.
ww.Put everything on a credit card until th: Putting everything on credit adds debt and interest for a want, with no plan to repay. Needs come first and debt should be avoided.

rw: Gross income is the total earned from wages and other sources before taxes and deductions, so it is always larger than net income.

ww.The amount saved each month for emergenc: Money saved for emergencies is savings, not income. Gross income is the total earned before anything is subtracted.
ww.The amount left after paying taxes and d: The amount left after taxes and deductions is net income, or take home pay. Gross income is the total before those are removed.
ww.The amount spent on needs each month by: Spending on needs is an expense category and says nothing about total income earned. Gross income is the full amount before deductions.

rw: Net income, or take home pay, equals gross pay minus taxes and deductions such as insurance and retirement. It is what lands in your bank account.

ww.The amount an employer pays in payroll t: Payroll taxes paid by the employer are a business cost and are not what the employee takes home. Net income is the employee's pay after deductions.
ww.The total amount earned before any deduc: The total before deductions is gross income. Net income is lower because taxes and deductions have already been subtracted.
ww.The amount of a yearly bonus paid out to: A yearly bonus is extra pay on top of wages. It is a type of earnings, not a measure of pay after deductions.

rw: Gross pay equals hourly rate times hours worked: $20 x 30 = $600. This is before taxes and deductions are taken out.

ww.$150: $150 is wrong; it comes from adding 20 + 30 times 3 or a similar error. Pay is rate times hours: $20 x 30 = $600.
ww.$6,000: $6,000 is ten times too large and likely a misplaced zero. Maya earns $20 x 30 hours = $600.
ww.$50: $50 is the sum of the rate and the hours (20 + 30). Pay must be multiplied: $20 x 30 = $600.

rw: Overtime at 1.5 times the regular rate means $16 x 1.5 = $24 per hour. It applies to hours over 40 in a week under U.S. wage law.

ww.$16 per hour: $16 is the regular rate, which has no overtime premium added. Overtime is time and a half, which is 1.5 x $16 = $24.
ww.$17.50 per hour: $17.50 does not match the 1.5 multiplier. It appears to add a flat amount, while 1.5 x $16 is exactly $24.
ww.$32 per hour: $32 is double time (2 x $16), not time and a half. The problem says 1.5 times, so the rate is $24 per hour.

rw: The W-4 tells an employer the employee's filing status and adjustments so the correct amount of federal income tax is withheld from pay.

ww.Reporting total yearly wages to the IRS: Reporting yearly wages to the IRS is done by the W-2 the employer files and gives the worker. The W-4 is completed by the employee.
ww.Requesting a tax refund from the IRS in: A refund is requested by filing a tax return (Form 1040). The W-4 only affects how much is withheld from each paycheck.
ww.Applying for a credit card at a bank or: A W-4 is an employment tax form, not a credit application. Credit cards use their own applications that check credit history.

rw: The W-2 is sent by employers each January and reports total wages for the year plus taxes withheld, which workers use to file their tax returns.

ww.A form that reports income for independe: Income for independent contractors is reported on a 1099, not a W-2. The W-2 is for employees.
ww.A form for applying for a job at a firm: Applying for a job uses a job application, not a W-2. The W-2 is a tax document issued after a person has worked for the employer.
ww.A form that sets the federal tax withhel: Withholding is set by the employee's W-4. The W-2 is the year end report that shows the wages and taxes that were actually withheld.

rw: FICA stands for the Federal Insurance Contributions Act. It is withheld from paychecks at 7.65 percent (6.2 Social Security plus 1.45 Medicare), matched by the employer.

ww.Property tax: Property tax is paid by owners of real estate to local governments and is not taken from paychecks to fund Social Security or Medicare.
ww.Sales tax: Sales tax is added at the register when buying goods. It is not withheld from wages and does not fund Social Security.
ww.Excise tax: Excise taxes apply to specific goods like gasoline or tobacco. They are not withheld from paychecks for Social Security and Medicare.

rw: A tip is money a customer gives for good service on top of the bill. It is common in restaurants and counts as taxable income.

ww.A fixed monthly salary paid by an employ: A fixed monthly pay is a salary, not a tip. A tip is extra money from a customer, not a set payment from an employer.
ww.A short-term loan from the employer to t: A short term loan from an employer is an advance. A tip is a gift of money from a customer and is never repaid.
ww.A payment made by the government to serv: Government payments to workers are wages or benefits. A tip comes from customers, not from the government, and is taxable income.

rw: Employers withhold income tax and payroll taxes for employees. Independent contractors get a 1099 and handle their own taxes, including self employment tax.

ww.Employees pay no income taxes on their w: Employees do pay income taxes on wages, usually through withholding. Saying they pay none is false, so it cannot be the difference.
ww.Contractors always earn more than employ: Contractors do not always earn more than employees; earnings vary by job, and contractors also pay their own taxes and often get no benefits.
ww.Employees always get to choose their own: Employees often have schedules set by employers, while contractors usually control their own hours. So employees do not always choose their hours.

rw: Rent from property you own is passive income, because it arrives from an asset with little ongoing work compared with a job.

ww.Wages earned from a full-time job: Wages from a full time job are earned income because you trade your time and labor for pay. They are not passive.
ww.Tips earned from serving tables daily: Tips come from serving customers, which is active work. This makes them earned income, not passive income.
ww.Pay earned for babysitting on weekends: Babysitting pay is earned by working, so it is active income. Passive income comes from assets like rentals or investments.

rw: Earned income is money received for work, such as wages, salaries, tips and self employment pay. A part time job pays wages.

ww.Interest on a savings account: Interest on savings comes from money in an account, not from work, so it is investment income, not earned income.
ww.Rent from a rental property: Rent from a rental property is passive income from an asset. Earned income is paid for work done.
ww.Dividends from stock shares: Dividends are payments from owning stock shares, which makes them investment income rather than earned income from work.

rw: A bonus is extra pay above regular wages, given for strong performance, meeting goals or company results. It is still taxable income.

ww.A loan advanced by the employer against: A loan advanced against future pay is a pay advance, which must be repaid. A bonus is extra pay that does not need repayment.
ww.A tax that is taken out of every paychec: A tax taken from every paycheck is a payroll or income tax deduction. A bonus adds to pay and is not a tax.
ww.A fixed amount deducted from pay for hea: A fixed deduction for health insurance is a premium withheld from pay. A bonus increases a paycheck rather than reducing it.

rw: A commission is pay based on a percentage of the sales a worker makes, which rewards selling more and is common in sales jobs.

ww.Pay based on the number of hours worked: Pay based on the number of hours worked is an hourly wage. A commission depends on sales results, not time.
ww.Pay that is given as a gift from the bos: A holiday gift from the boss is a gift or bonus, not a commission, which is earned from sales.
ww.Pay based on a fixed amount for the whol: A fixed yearly amount is a salary. A commission varies with sales, so it can be higher or lower from month to month.

rw: Commission is rate times sales: 0.04 x $25,000 = $1,000. This pay is earned in addition to or instead of a base salary.

ww.$4,000: $4,000 is 16 percent of $25,000. The rate here is 4 percent, so the commission is much less than that.
ww.$10,000: $10,000 is 40 percent of the sales. The commission rate is 4 percent, which gives $1,000.
ww.$100: $100 is only 0.4 percent of $25,000, a tenth of the right amount. Four percent of $25,000 is $1,000.

rw: Employer paid health insurance can be worth thousands of dollars per year in premiums, so it is among the most valuable benefits a job can offer.

ww.A free parking sign nearby: A parking sign gives no real financial value; it only marks a spot and does not pay for anything the worker would otherwise buy.
ww.A company logo mug as a gift: A logo mug is a small gift worth only a few dollars, far below the value of benefits that replace thousands in costs.
ww.A holiday card from the boss: A holiday card is a kind gesture with almost no financial worth, so it is not a major benefit.

rw: A 401(k) match means the employer adds money, often a percentage of what the employee contributes. It is free retirement savings and worth taking in full.

ww.The employer charges a fee for joining t: A match is a benefit, not a fee. Charges for joining a plan are plan fees, which are separate from an employer's contribution.
ww.The employer takes money from the employ: Employee contributions come out of pay by the employee's choice. A match adds employer money; it never takes money away from the account.
ww.The employer lends the employee money fo: A match is a contribution, not a loan, and the employer does not lend retirement money. The employee does not have to repay it.

rw: A minimum wage is the lowest hourly pay an employer may legally pay most covered workers. The federal rate is $7.25 and states can set higher rates.

ww.The highest hourly pay an employer may g: The minimum wage is the lowest pay allowed, not the highest. Employers may pay above the minimum wage, so it is not a cap.
ww.The pay that applies to workers who rece: Tipped workers are covered by minimum wage rules too, with tip credit rules, so a minimum wage is not limited to tipped workers.
ww.The pay that applies to managers and exe: Minimum wage laws protect hourly workers at the low end of pay. They are not limited to managers or executives, who usually earn salaries.

rw: Education builds knowledge and skills that employers value, so educated workers tend to qualify for higher paying roles and earn more over time.

ww.Education guarantees a job without any f: Education does not guarantee a job. Workers still need to find employment and perform well, so a promise of a guaranteed job is false.
ww.Education reduces the need to work for a: Education does not remove the need to work. People still need income, and education only improves how much they can earn.
ww.Education lowers the amount of taxes a p: Education does not reduce taxes. Higher earners may in fact pay more tax, so this is not why education raises earning potential.

rw: A side hustle is extra work done outside a main job to earn additional income, such as freelancing, tutoring or reselling goods.

ww.A tax form that is used only for extra j: A tax form is a document like a 1099 or W-4. A side hustle is the work itself, not a form, though its income may need reporting.
ww.A promotion at work to a higher position: A promotion is a move to a higher position within the same job. A side hustle is separate work done for extra income.
ww.A loan from a friend to cover expenses: A loan from a friend is borrowed money that must be repaid, not earned income. A side hustle brings in new income by working.

rw: The teen earned the money as self employed, so the teen is responsible for tracking and reporting it. Net earnings of $400 or more usually require filing.

ww.No one, because lawn mowing is exempt un: Lawn mowing income is not exempt. Self employment earnings are generally taxable, and income of $400 or more triggers self employment tax filing.
ww.The city government where the teen lives: A city government does not report a person's private earnings. The person who earned the money is responsible for reporting it.
ww.The customers who paid for the mowing an: Customers who pay for services generally do not report on behalf of a worker for small jobs. The worker must report their own income.

rw: A pay stub shows gross pay, each deduction (taxes, insurance, retirement) and net pay for a pay period, helping workers check their paycheck is correct.

ww.A bill that is sent to the employee each: A bill is a request for payment. A pay stub is given to an employee to show how a paycheck was calculated.
ww.A tax return filed at the end of the yea: A tax return is filed once a year with the government. A pay stub comes with each paycheck and shows pay details only.
ww.A job application filled out by a candid: A job application is filled out before being hired. A pay stub is given after work is done and pay is issued.

rw: Net pay equals gross pay minus deductions: $800 - $120 - $30 = $650. This take home amount is what the employee actually receives.

ww.$770: $770 only subtracts the $30 insurance and ignores the $120 in taxes. Both deductions must come out of the $800 gross.
ww.$950: $950 adds the deductions to gross pay instead of subtracting them. Deductions reduce pay, so net must be less than $800.
ww.$680: $680 subtracts only the taxes ($800 - $120) and misses the $30 insurance deduction. Both amounts must be taken from gross pay.

rw: A need is essential for living, such as food, shelter and basic clothing, while a want is something you would like but can live without.

ww.A want is something that is required by: Laws do not require wants for everyone. A want is something nice to have, while a need is essential, like food or shelter.
ww.A need is something that you must save u: A need is not something to save up for first; needs like food and housing must be met right away, before wants.
ww.A need always costs less money than a wa: Cost does not define a need. A need can be expensive, such as rent, and a want can be cheap, so cost does not separate them.

rw: Comparing prices and features from several sellers helps you find the best value and avoid overpaying for a large purchase.

ww.Borrow the money before researching the: Borrowing before researching commits you to debt and interest without knowing if the product is right or fairly priced.
ww.Ask a friend to buy it for you at their: Asking a friend to buy it for you at their store is not a research step and does not help you find the best price or quality.
ww.Buy from the first store that you happen: Buying from the first store you visit skips any comparison, so you may pay more than necessary for the same item.

rw: Unit pricing is the cost per unit of measure, such as per ounce or per pound, which makes items of different sizes easy to compare.

ww.The shipping cost charged for each onlin: Shipping costs are an added fee for delivery. Unit pricing divides the price by the quantity to find the cost per unit.
ww.The total cost of one whole shopping tri: The total cost of a shopping trip is the sum of everything bought. Unit pricing is per item or measure, not an overall total.
ww.The tax that is added at the store check: Sales tax is added at checkout based on a percentage of the price. Unit price is the price divided by the amount, not a tax.

rw: The 24 oz bottle costs $4.20 / 24 = $0.175 per ounce, versus $3.20 / 16 = $0.20 for the small bottle. So the larger one is the better value.

ww.It cannot be determined by anyone: The answer can be determined with simple division: price divided by ounces gives each bottle's cost per ounce.
ww.They are exactly equal per ounce: They are not equal: $3.20 / 16 = $0.20 per ounce and $4.20 / 24 = $0.175 per ounce, so the larger bottle costs less per ounce.
ww.The 16 oz bottle at $0.20 per ounce now: The 16 oz bottle does cost $0.20 per ounce ($3.20 / 16), but that is higher than the $0.175 per ounce of the 24 oz bottle, so it is not the better deal.

rw: Impulse buying is making an unplanned purchase on a sudden urge, often driven by emotion, displays or sales, rather than a real need.

ww.Waiting a week before buying anything at: Waiting a week before buying is the opposite of impulse buying. It is a strategy to avoid acting on a sudden urge.
ww.Buying only what is on a planned list at: Buying only items on a planned list is disciplined shopping, the opposite of impulse buying.
ww.Comparing prices before buying anything: Comparing prices before buying is planned shopping and the opposite of impulse buying, which happens without thought or comparison.

rw: Waiting a day gives time for the urge to pass and lets you judge if the item is truly needed, which prevents impulse buys.

ww.Saving credit card numbers in every app: Saving card numbers in every app makes purchases quick and easy, which encourages impulse buying instead of preventing it.
ww.Shopping when you are bored or in a bad: Shopping when bored or upset leads to emotional spending, which increases impulse purchases rather than preventing them.
ww.Ignoring your budget when you shop in th: Ignoring your budget makes overspending easy. A budget helps prevent impulse buying by setting limits, so ignoring it does the opposite.

rw: Entertainment spending changes from month to month depending on choices, so it is a variable expense that can be adjusted when budgeting.

ww.A car loan payment due every month: A car loan payment is the same amount each month under the loan agreement, which makes it a fixed expense rather than a variable one.
ww.Monthly rent for an apartment or house: Rent is set by a lease and stays the same each month, so it is a fixed expense, not a variable one.
ww.A monthly insurance premium on a policy: Insurance premiums are set amounts due on a regular schedule, making them fixed expenses and not variable.

rw: Monthly rent is a set amount due each month under a lease, so it is a fixed expense that is easy to plan for.

ww.Clothing bills: Clothing spending changes with needs and choices from month to month, which makes it variable rather than fixed.
ww.Grocery spending: Grocery spending changes with prices, household size and shopping habits, so it is a variable expense, not a fixed one.
ww.Gas for a car: Gas costs depend on how much you drive and on fuel prices, so they vary each month and are not a fixed expense.

rw: Cutting snack spending frees money, and putting the difference toward savings improves the balance between wants and savings, which tracking is meant to reveal.

ww.Increase snack spending, since other cos: Increasing snack spending would worsen the imbalance. Snacks are a flexible want, so claiming other costs cannot be cut does not justify spending more.
ww.Borrow money to cover snacks and other s: Borrowing for snacks creates debt and interest for a want. It makes the problem worse rather than solving it.
ww.Stop tracking spending to avoid stress a: Tracking is what shows where money goes. Stopping it hides the problem and prevents the student from making better choices.

rw: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative given up, so it is what else the $50 could have bought or funded.

ww.The shipping cost for the order of the g: Shipping is a direct cost, a price paid, not the value of the best alternative given up. Opportunity cost is about the forgone option.
ww.The $50 price tag of the video game itse: The $50 price tag is the money cost. Opportunity cost is the other use of that $50 that you gave up to buy the game.
ww.The sales tax paid on the game at checko: Sales tax is part of the actual price paid. Opportunity cost is the best alternative given up, not an added charge.

rw: A warranty is a seller's or manufacturer's promise to repair or replace a product with defects for a stated time, protecting the buyer.

ww.A coupon that gives a discount on the it: A coupon is a discount offer for a future purchase. A warranty is a promise about product quality and repair.
ww.A store rule that stops all returns afte: A store rule limiting returns is a return policy, which is different from a warranty, which covers defects after purchase.
ww.A tax that is charged on the products yo: Sales tax is a government charge added at checkout. A warranty is a seller's or maker's promise about the product.

rw: Many free trials renew into paid plans automatically if not canceled. Check the renewal terms, price and how to cancel before giving your card.

ww.Whether the logo is attractive and eye-c: A logo says nothing about cost or terms. Looks do not tell you whether you will be charged after the trial ends.
ww.Whether friends have used it before you: Other people's use does not show whether you will be billed. The trial terms are what matter, not popularity.
ww.Nothing, because free trials are always: Free trials are not always free; many convert to paid subscriptions and charge the card on file unless you cancel in time.

rw: A return policy states when and how a store accepts returns or exchanges, including time limits, receipts and refund type.

ww.A law that forces stores to refund all p: No law forces stores to refund all purchases. Return policies are mostly set by each store, with some state rules.
ww.A tax on returned items that a store col: A return policy is not a tax. Stores do not collect a yearly tax on returned items, so this option is made up.
ww.A rule about advertising that a store ha: Advertising rules are set by laws and agencies. A return policy deals with returns and exchanges, not advertising.

rw: Buying from secure, reputable sites (look for https) and checking reviews lowers the risk of fraud and gives you better recourse if something goes wrong.

ww.Clicking links in unsolicited emails fro: Clicking links in unsolicited emails is risky because they often lead to phishing sites that steal your information.
ww.Sending money by gift cards to a seller: Scammers ask for gift cards because they are untraceable and hard to recover, so paying a stranger that way is a classic sign of fraud.
ww.Sharing your password with the seller to: Sharing your password lets someone take over your account and steal your information, so never share it with a seller.

rw: A sales tax is a percentage added to the price of goods and services at the time of purchase, collected by the seller for the state or local government.

ww.A tax charged on gifts people give: Gifts may be subject to a gift tax in some cases, but that is separate from a sales tax, which applies when buying goods.
ww.A tax charged on income earned: A tax on income earned is an income tax, collected on wages and other earnings, not a sales tax added at purchase.
ww.A tax charged on property owned: A tax on owned property is a property tax, usually paid yearly by owners of homes or land, not a sales tax.

rw: Sales tax is price times rate: $60 x 0.08 = $4.80. Total price is $60 + $4.80 = $64.80, which is what the customer pays at checkout.

ww.$60.80: $60.80 adds only 80 cents, which would be a 1.33 percent tax. Eight percent of $60 is $4.80, so the total is $64.80.
ww.$68.00: $68.00 adds $8, which is a tax of about 13.3 percent. The rate is 8 percent, so $4.80 is added, giving $64.80.
ww.$48.00: $48.00 subtracts 20 percent from the price instead of adding 8 percent tax. Tax raises the price, so the total is above $60.

rw: Saving prepares you for emergencies and future goals, like a car, school or retirement, and reduces the need to borrow.

ww.It guarantees you will never need a job: Saving does not guarantee you never need a job. Savings can run out, and most people need ongoing income.
ww.It makes you spend more money on things: Saving means spending less now, not more. Putting money aside lets it be used for later needs and goals.
ww.It removes the need for a budget in your: Saving does not remove the need for a budget; a budget is the tool that helps you decide how much to save.

rw: An emergency fund is money set aside for unexpected costs such as car repairs, medical bills or job loss, so you can avoid borrowing.

ww.Money that is borrowed to pay for emerge: Borrowed money is debt that must be repaid with interest. An emergency fund is your own saved money.
ww.Money invested in stocks in order to gro: Investments in stocks can lose value quickly, so they are not suited for an emergency fund, which needs to be safe and available.
ww.Money that is set aside for a vacation n: Money for a vacation is a planned savings goal. An emergency fund covers unexpected costs, not planned trips.

rw: A savings account is safe, usually FDIC insured, and lets you withdraw quickly, which fits an emergency fund that must be available.

ww.In a long-term account that charges pena: A long term account with withdrawal penalties makes the money hard to reach in an emergency, so it is a poor place for the fund.
ww.Under a mattress at home where thieves m: Cash at home earns no interest and can be lost, stolen or destroyed. It is not as safe as an insured bank account.
ww.In a risky stock that could lose its val: A risky stock can lose value just when you need the money, so it is the wrong place for an emergency fund.

rw: Interest is the money a bank pays you for keeping your money there, because the bank lends out deposits and shares part of its earnings.

ww.A fee that you pay each time you withdra: A fee for ATM withdrawals is a bank charge, not interest. Interest is money the bank pays you.
ww.The amount of money that you deposit in: The money deposited is called the principal. Interest is what the bank pays on top of that for using your money.
ww.A tax that is charged on your savings ea: Interest on savings is earned by you, not charged. A tax on savings would be a different concept, and interest itself may be taxable income.

rw: Compound interest is earned on the original deposit plus interest already earned, so growth speeds up over time. This is why early saving matters.

ww.Interest that is paid only when a person: Interest paid only at retirement is not compound interest. Compounding adds interest to the balance on a regular schedule.
ww.Interest that decreases a little each ye: Compound interest does not shrink each year; because it builds on a growing balance, the interest amount tends to rise over time.
ww.Interest that is earned only on the orig: Interest only on the original deposit is simple interest. Compound interest also earns interest on previous interest.

rw: With the same rate, the account that compounds most often adds interest to the balance more frequently, so it grows the most over 10 years.

ww.The one with no interest paid: An account with no interest would not grow at all, so it would grow the least of the group, not the most.
ww.The one that pays simple interest: Simple interest only earns on the original deposit, so it grows more slowly than an account that compounds interest on interest.
ww.The one with the highest fees only: High fees reduce the balance, so an account with the highest fees would grow the least, not the most.

rw: Starting early gives compound interest more time to build, so each dollar saved early grows much more by retirement.

ww.Banks always pay younger savers higher r: Banks do not always pay younger savers higher rates; rates depend on the account and market, not the saver's age.
ww.You can spend all of your income right a: Spending all income right away is the opposite of saving. Starting to save early is about setting money aside.
ww.You will never need to save any money ag: You will always need to save over a lifetime, since expenses continue. Starting early only makes the saving easier.

rw: A CD holds money for a set term at a fixed rate, and early withdrawal usually brings a penalty. It is generally FDIC insured.

ww.A stock that pays dividends every quarte: A stock that pays dividends is an ownership share, not a CD. A CD is a deposit with a bank, not a stock.
ww.A loan from a bank that must be repaid i: A loan repaid in monthly parts is an installment loan. A CD is a deposit that earns interest for you.
ww.A checking account that allows unlimited: A checking account allows frequent withdrawals. A CD locks money for a set term, which is why it pays a higher rate.

rw: FDIC insurance protects bank deposits up to $250,000 per depositor, per bank, per ownership category if the bank fails.

ww.Cash that is kept in a drawer at home fo: Cash kept at home is not in a bank, so FDIC insurance does not cover it if it is lost or stolen.
ww.Stocks that you own through a broker or: Stocks held through a broker are not covered by FDIC insurance and can lose value. Brokerage accounts may have SIPC coverage for broker failure only.
ww.Your credit score at the credit bureaus: Credit scores are tracked by credit bureaus, and FDIC insurance has nothing to do with them. It covers bank deposits.

rw: The standard FDIC limit is $250,000 per depositor, per bank, per ownership category, so $250,000 of the $300,000 is insured and $50,000 is not.

ww.$300,000: $300,000 is the whole balance, but FDIC insurance has a limit per depositor, per bank, per ownership category, so the entire amount is not insured.
ww.$50,000: $50,000 is an old, lower figure that does not match today's limit. The standard limit is $250,000.
ww.$100,000: $100,000 was the limit before 2008 and no longer applies. Today's standard limit is $250,000.

rw: A savings goal is a specific amount you plan to save by a certain date, such as $600 in six months, which gives you something to aim for.

ww.A required bill that comes in every mont: A required monthly bill is a fixed expense. A savings goal is something you choose to work toward.
ww.A plan for repaying a loan over time in: A plan for repaying a loan is a repayment schedule. A savings goal is about building money, not paying off debt.
ww.A fee that is charged by a bank for an a: A bank fee is a charge for services. A savings goal is a target amount you set for yourself.

rw: Monthly savings equal the goal divided by months: $600 / 6 = $100. Saving that amount each month for 6 months reaches the $600 goal.

ww.$3,600: $3,600 is $600 times 6, which multiplies instead of dividing. The monthly amount must be $600 split over 6 months.
ww.$36: $36 is far too small; it would only reach $216 after 6 months. Dividing $600 by 6 gives the right monthly amount.
ww.$60: $60 a month for 6 months totals only $360, which falls short of $600. The goal requires $600 / 6 = $100 a month.

rw: Pay yourself first means moving money into savings as soon as you are paid, before spending on other things, so saving becomes a habit.

ww.Skipping saving so you can spend a lot m: Skipping saving to spend more is the opposite of paying yourself first, which puts saving ahead of spending.
ww.Spending on wants before you pay the bil: Spending on wants before bills is risky and not what pay yourself first means; it is about saving, not wants.
ww.Borrowing money to give yourself a rewar: Borrowing for a reward adds debt. Paying yourself first uses your own income, moved to savings before other spending.

rw: Automatic saving sets up regular transfers into savings, often each payday, so saving happens without relying on willpower.

ww.Withdrawing money from savings every wee: Withdrawing money from savings every week would drain the account. Automatic saving adds money, it does not take it out.
ww.Closing the savings account once a year: Closing the account once a year does not build savings. Automatic saving keeps the account open and growing.
ww.Spending money automatically on small it: Automatic spending on small items is the opposite of saving. Automatic saving moves money into savings, not out for purchases.

rw: Dividing 72 by the annual interest rate estimates the years it takes money to double. At 8 percent, money doubles in about 9 years.

ww.Setting the age at which a person must r: The Rule of 72 does not set a retirement age. It estimates how long it takes for money to double.
ww.Finding the monthly payment on a loan: Loan payments are found with payment formulas or calculators. The Rule of 72 only estimates doubling time for growth.
ww.Calculating the taxes owed on income: Taxes owed are found using tax tables and rates. The Rule of 72 estimates how long money takes to double.

rw: Years to double is about 72 divided by the rate: 72 / 4 = 18 years. A higher rate would shorten that time.

ww.72 years: 72 years is the number 72 itself, not divided by the rate. The Rule of 72 divides 72 by the interest rate.
ww.30 years: 30 years does not match the rule. Dividing 72 by 4 gives 18, so money doubles in about 18 years at 4 percent.
ww.4 years: 4 years is just the rate itself. The rule divides 72 by 4, which gives 18 years, not 4.

rw: A high yield savings account pays a higher interest rate than a regular savings account, often at online banks, and is typically FDIC insured.

ww.A stock account used to trade shares: A stock account is a brokerage account used to trade shares, not a savings account, and it is not FDIC insured.
ww.A checking account that pays no interest: A checking account that pays no interest is not a high yield account. High yield means a higher interest rate on savings.
ww.A loan that charges a high interest rate: A loan that charges high interest is a borrowing product. A high yield savings account pays you interest.

rw: Inflation raises prices, so cash buys less over time. Cash that is not growing loses purchasing power.

ww.The cash earns interest automatically: Cash kept as cash earns no interest. Only money in an interest paying account earns interest.
ww.The cash doubles each year on its own: Cash does not grow on its own. It stays the same amount while prices rise, so it loses value in real terms.
ww.Purchasing power increases over time: Inflation reduces purchasing power rather than increasing it, because the same amount buys fewer goods as prices go up.

rw: Real value falls because inflation (3 percent) is higher than interest (1 percent). The real return is about 1 - 3 = negative 2 percent a year.

ww.It is doubling every year on its own wit: Savings do not double every year on their own. At 1 percent interest, the balance grows very slowly.
ww.It is staying exactly the same, as nothi: The balance grows by 1 percent, but prices rise 3 percent, so the real value is not staying the same.
ww.It is increasing because interest earned: Interest is positive, but real value depends on inflation too. With prices up 3 percent and interest only 1 percent, buying power declines.

rw: A 529 plan is a tax advantaged account for education costs, with tax free growth and withdrawals when used for qualified expenses.

ww.To buy individual stocks only, with no o: A 529 plan is designed for education savings, not for buying individual stocks only, though funds may be invested.
ww.To save for family vacations only, and f: A 529 plan is meant for education, not family vacations. Using it for non education costs can bring taxes and penalties.
ww.To pay off credit card bills each month: A 529 plan is for education costs, not paying off credit cards. Credit card payments are not qualified expenses.

rw: Savings accounts usually pay interest, while many checking accounts pay little or none, which is the main reason to keep savings there.

ww.Savings accounts allow unlimited checks: Savings accounts do not allow unlimited checks. Checking accounts are the ones made for frequent payments and check writing.
ww.Savings accounts require no deposits: Deposits are needed to build savings. A savings account is not defined by requiring no deposits.
ww.Savings accounts have no safety at all: Savings accounts are usually FDIC insured, so claiming they have no safety at all is false.
